subtype: Restless at work and searching for stimulation [Actor]
passage:
Devika, you asked what I actually do all day at the bank. Honestly? Last Tuesday, just before Diwali, I counted. I checked the cricket score eleven times. I sorted my desktop icons by colour. I refilled my water bottle six times just to walk somewhere. I read about a volcano in Iceland for forty minutes.
My real work, approving the same three kinds of forms, takes maybe two hours. The rest I fill with bits. Tiny distractions, one after another.
And the weird part is, I go home feeling guilty. Like I stole the day. Nobody's complaining. My manager thinks I'm great. But I, Akash, feel like I'm slowly going dull.
I keep wondering if I'm tired, or bored because it's too easy, or if none of it means anything to me. Maybe all three. I need to work out which, before I spend my whole life checking scores.

qa.q: How many times did Akash check the cricket score last Tuesday?
qa.a: Eleven times.

qa.q: How does Akash feel at the end of the day?
qa.a: Akash feels vaguely guilty, "like I stole the day", and uneasy about going dull, even though nobody is complaining.

qa.q: What could Akash do with this boredom?
qa.a: Work out its cause: if the work is too easy, ask for harder projects; if it lacks meaning, look for work that matters to Akash; if it is tiredness, rest properly.

qa.q: How does Akash's manager seem to see things?
qa.a: The manager thinks Akash is great, probably because the forms get done, without seeing the restlessness underneath.

grounding: An adult who is not challenged at work fills the day with small distractions, feels vaguely guilty, and wonders whether the boredom needs meaning, difficulty or rest.

subtype: Lost in a game or puzzle [Actor]
passage:
Winter holiday club, Day 3: carer's note.
Gautam spent the whole morning at the big construction set. He started a bridge between two tables, failed twice when it sagged in the middle, then added a triangle of pieces underneath and it held. I watched him mutter to himself, test it with a toy truck, and start a second, longer bridge.
At twelve Ishita called everyone for lunch. He didn't hear her. When I tapped his shoulder he looked up, blinking, as if waking. "Is it lunch already? I just started." He had been there two and a half hours.
He ate quickly and went straight back, calm and bright-eyed all afternoon.
Plan: tomorrow I will offer him a slightly harder bridge, one that can hold the heavier truck.

qa.q: What did Gautam add to make the bridge hold?
qa.a: A triangle of pieces underneath.

qa.q: What does "Is it lunch already? I just started" suggest about Gautam?
qa.a: Gautam was so absorbed and happy in the challenge that he lost track of time, and he stayed calm and bright-eyed afterwards.

qa.q: Why is the carer's plan a good next step?
qa.a: A slightly harder bridge keeps the challenge just above his skill, which is what kept him absorbed, without tipping into frustration.

qa.q: How might Ishita see Gautam not hearing the lunch call?
qa.a: Ishita might first think he was ignoring her, but seeing the bridges she would likely understand he was completely absorbed. 🙂

grounding: A carer notes a child so absorbed in building a bridge, with the challenge matching his skill, that he forgets lunch and time.

passage:
In the summer holidays the village ground outside Sehore baked by noon, so Avni practised bowling at six in the morning. Jahnavi Didi, who coached the girls' team, set up a single stump and a steel plate as a target on a good length.
The first twenty balls went everywhere. Then Avni shortened her run-up and something clicked. She hit the plate once. Then again. Each ball needed all her attention: her wrist, her front foot, the seam. It was hard, but just possible.
She forgot her phone in her bag. She forgot the heat, forgot the buffalo wandering past the boundary. When Jahnavi Didi finally called, "Avni, it's eight!", she looked up in surprise.
Walking home, her legs ached, but her head felt clear and quiet, like the pond after rain.

qa.q: What target did Jahnavi Didi set up?
qa.a: A single stump and a steel plate on a good length.

qa.q: How did Avni feel walking home?
qa.a: Avni felt calm and clear-headed, "like the pond after rain", even with aching legs, after two hours of full absorption.

qa.q: What made the practice absorbing rather than frustrating?
qa.a: A clear target and a task hard enough to need all her attention but just possible, especially once shortening the run-up let her start hitting the plate.

qa.q: What might Jahnavi Didi notice when Avni looks up in surprise?
qa.a: Jahnavi Didi probably sees a player so absorbed she lost two hours, a good sign the difficulty is set just right.

grounding: A teenager practising bowling forgets her phone and the time, and feels calm and clear afterwards, because the task is hard but possible.

passage:
Dear Yamini,
You asked how I suddenly finished the whole illustration series. It wasn't magic, I promise. I built it.
I used to wait for the mood. The mood came about twice a month, usually at midnight. So in March I changed three things.
One: every morning I write one clear goal on a card. Not "work on the series" but "ink the market scene background".
Two: 9 to 12 is closed. Phone in the other room, door shut, a note on it for Amma.
Three: I pick something just a little harder than I can comfortably do. This month it's crowds, which I used to avoid.
Most mornings now, I look up and it's twelve and I don't know where the time went. The crowd scene took four days and I loved every hour.
Try it with your music?
Nirmala

qa.q: Which hours does Nirmala keep closed?
How does Nirmala feel about working on the crowd scene?
qa.a: Nirmala loved every hour of it; the stretch felt absorbing and satisfying rather than frustrating. 😊

qa.q: Which of Nirmala's changes invite deep focus, and why?
qa.a: A clear daily goal, three uninterrupted hours, and tasks just above current skill together make deep focus likely, instead of waiting for a rare mood.

qa.q: What would change for Yamini if Yamini tried this with music?
qa.a: With one clear goal, protected time and a slightly hard piece to practise, Yamini might also stop waiting for the mood and lose track of time in work that feels good.

grounding: An adult builds the conditions for deep focus with clear goals, fewer interruptions and tasks slightly above current skill.

passage:
"Harsha, come, the kite's ready. Let's try again."
"Whatever."
"Whatever? It's Lohri tomorrow! Everyone's flying."
"I'll just crash it. I always crash it."
"You crashed it three times yesterday. That's how—"
"And Papa shouted every time. 'Pull, Harsha! Not like that! Why can't you do anything right?' I pull, it crashes. I don't pull, it crashes. Doesn't matter what I do."
"...He shouted that?"
"Every time. So I'll just watch."
"Okay. What if it's only you and me on the back roof? No shouting. I'll hold the string with you, and we just get it up. Just up."
"...It'll still crash."
"Maybe. Then we'll find out why. Come."
Gurpreet held out the spool and waited.

qa.q: How many times did Harsha crash the kite yesterday?
qa.a: Three times.

qa.q: Why does Harsha say "Whatever"?
qa.a: After being shouted at no matter what, Harsha feels defeated and hopeless; pulling or not, it crashes, so giving up seems the only sensible thing.

qa.q: What makes Gurpreet's offer a good next step?
qa.a: No shouting, holding the string together, and a tiny goal of "just up" give Harsha a chance to see that effort can change what happens.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet feel hearing what Papa said?
qa.a: Gurpreet seems taken aback and concerned, and wants to give Harsha a gentler, safer try.

grounding: A child who has been shouted at and keeps failing with a kite stops trying and says whatever, since effort seems to change nothing.

subtype: Not asking for help at home [Actor]
passage:
Sunday, Losar week

Dolma Aunty asked me again today what I want for the Losar dinner. "Anything you like, Uma. Momos? Your choice."
I said, "Whatever you're making, Aunty."
She's asked me things like this every week since I came to live here in March. What colour for my room. Which school club. Whether I want the window seat. I always say whatever, or I don't mind.
At home before, when I asked for things, nobody even looked up. Once I asked to go on the school trip and Papa just kept watching TV. After a while I stopped asking. It felt stupid to want things out loud.
Tonight she made momos anyway, and I ate six. I did want them. I just couldn't say it.
Maybe next week, if she asks, I'll try to say one real thing.

Uma

qa.q: What did Dolma Aunty ask Uma about the Losar dinner?
qa.a: What Uma wanted, "Anything you like", suggesting momos.

qa.q: Why does Uma keep saying "whatever"?
qa.a: Uma learned at home that asking changed nothing, so wanting things out loud feels stupid and risky, even though Uma really did want the momos.

qa.q: How could Dolma Aunty help Uma start voicing wishes?
qa.a: Keep asking gently, offer two simple choices, and warmly act on any small wish Uma names, so Uma sees that speaking up makes a difference here.

qa.q: What might Dolma Aunty feel when Uma always says "whatever"?
qa.a: Dolma Aunty may feel puzzled or a little sad, wanting to please Uma but getting no clue; making momos anyway shows she keeps trying.

grounding: A teenager whose wishes were ignored at home no longer voices them, even in a new home where someone keeps asking.

passage:
At the evening computer class in the kasba of Rampur, Sangeeta Ma'am handed out the spreadsheet exercise. Pooja, nineteen, looked at it and put her pen down before reading the second line. "Ma'am, I can't do this. I'm not a computer person. I'll only mess it up."
Sangeeta Ma'am had watched her in the first week sorting her father's shop accounts in a notebook, quick and neat. She didn't argue. She took the sheet back and gave Pooja a smaller one: type the shop's five items and their prices into five boxes.
Pooja did it in three minutes. "That's it?"
"Now ask it to add them." Sangeeta Ma'am showed her the one button.
The total appeared. Pooja checked it against her notebook, twice. It matched. She looked up, and for the first time that week asked, "Can I try the next part?"

qa.q: What was the smaller task Sangeeta Ma'am gave Pooja?
qa.a: Type the shop's five items and their prices into five boxes.

qa.q: What might Sangeeta Ma'am have been thinking when Pooja said "I can't do this"?
qa.a: She seemed calm and quietly confident in Pooja, remembering how quick and neat Pooja was with the shop accounts, so she chose a small win over an argument.

qa.q: Why did the smaller task work?
qa.a: It was easy enough to succeed at quickly, and checking the total against her own notebook gave Pooja real evidence that her effort worked, so she wanted the next part.

qa.q: How did Pooja's view of herself shift?
qa.a: Pooja moved from "I'm not a computer person" to asking for the next part, as one success loosened the belief that trying was useless.

grounding: A teacher sees a capable student give up before starting and sets a small task she can succeed at, which begins to break the belief that effort is useless.

subtype: Stuck in an unresponsive job or home [Actor]
passage:
By July, winter in Buenos Aires, Camila had stopped writing to her manager. She had asked for a second screen in February, for help with the backlog in March, for a day off for her sister's graduation in May. No reply, no reply, a "we'll see" that never came back.
Now she came in, did her tickets, and left. When her headset broke, she held the loose earpiece to her ear for a week instead of asking. At home she lay on the sofa with the TV on, not watching.
One Sunday Gabriel, her flatmate, sat down beside her. "You used to fight for everything. Now you don't even say when you're cold."
"What's the point? Nothing I ask for happens."
"At work, maybe. But you've seemed flat for weeks now. Would you talk to someone, a doctor or a counsellor? I'll sit with you while you call tomorrow."
Camila shrugged, but she didn't say no.

qa.q: What did Camila ask for in February?
qa.a: A second screen.

qa.q: Why has Camila stopped asking for anything?
qa.a: After months of ignored requests, Camila feels numb and hopeless ("What's the point?"), so asking seems useless, even when the headset breaks.

qa.q: What is a sensible next step for Camila?
qa.a: Since the flatness has lasted for weeks, talking to a doctor or counsellor, as Gabriel suggests, is wise; the ignored requests could also go to someone above the manager.

qa.q: How does Gabriel see the change in Camila?
qa.a: Gabriel remembers someone who "used to fight for everything" and is worried to see her flat for weeks, so he offers to sit with her while she calls.

grounding: An adult whose every request at work was ignored stops asking and feels numb, and a flatmate suggests talking to a qualified professional.

passage:
Simran, you see that jamun tree by the gate? Your Uday Dadaji planted it when he was nine. That monsoon my father gave me a seed and said, "You choose where it goes." I chose that corner, where rainwater ran off the roof. Every day after school I checked. Nothing. Two weeks, nothing. I almost gave up.
Then one morning, a little green loop pushing through the mud. I shouted so loudly the neighbours came. I chose the spot, I watered it, and it grew. After that, when my cycle chain broke, I didn't cry for my father. I tried fixing it myself.
So, beta, which pot do you want for your tulsi? You choose.

qa.q: Where did young Uday plant the jamun seed?
qa.a: In the corner by the gate where rainwater ran off the roof.

qa.q: How did young Uday feel when the green loop appeared?
qa.a: He felt thrilled and proud, shouting so loudly the neighbours came, because his own choice and care had made it grow.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: His father letting him choose the spot; seeing his choice and watering produce a shoot taught him his actions mattered, so later he tried fixing his cycle chain himself.

qa.q: How might Uday's father have felt watching the seed come up?
qa.a: His father probably felt quietly pleased, having handed over the choice on purpose and seeing his son learn that effort changes things.

grounding: An elder recalls choosing where to plant a seed as a child and seeing it grow, which taught him that his actions mattered.

passage:
In Udvada that winter, Zubin's father's bakery had closed, and the house was full of low voices at night. Zubin couldn't sleep, couldn't study, and snapped at everyone.
At school, Lakshmi Miss noticed him staring at a blank page and kept him back after class. She drew a line down the middle of a sheet. "Left side: what you can't change. Right side: what you can."
Left: the bakery. Papa's worry. The money.
Right, after a long pause: when I study. Helping Mamma with dinner. Talking to someone instead of snapping. Bed at ten.
"Pick one from the right for this week," she said. "Come and tell me how it went on Friday."
He picked studying after dinner at the kitchen table, where he could hear his parents. On Friday he told her he had managed four nights out of five. For the first time in weeks, he felt a little less helpless.

qa.q: What did Zubin write first on the "can't change" side?
qa.a: The bakery.

qa.q: How did Zubin feel by Friday?
qa.a: Zubin felt a little less helpless for the first time in weeks, because acting on one thing he could control gave back some sense of power.

qa.q: Why did Lakshmi Miss's two-column sheet help?
qa.a: Separating what can't be changed from what can let Zubin stop fighting the impossible and put his energy into one small, doable action, with a Friday check-in for support.

qa.q: How might Zubin's parents experience him studying at the kitchen table?
qa.a: His parents may feel a little comforted to see him calmer and close by while they deal with the bakery closing. 🤍

grounding: A teenager facing a hard family situation lists what he can and cannot control, and acting on the first list restores some sense of power.
